title: Whom to Honour: Decorating an HVO Formation
sources: ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), 29 May 2013, HVO command and conduct findings
ICTY Kordić & Čerkez Trial Judgment (IT-95-14/2-T), HVO organisation in central Bosnia
content:
For the leadership of Herceg-Bosna, a decoration was a leadership gesture that carried more risk than its modest occasion suggested. To single out one steadfast formation, to issue a broad citation across the regular HVO, or to decline amid heavy losses appeared to be a simple matter of recognising service. But the HVO's record, examined in detail at the ICTY, was uneven, and some units associated with the central Bosnia fighting were implicated in conduct the tribunals named as crimes. An honour does not discriminate; it lands on the whole of a formation's history.

This essay treats the decoration as a morale instrument and declines the language of glory. A leadership that honours a unit makes itself answerable for that unit's conduct; the citation meant to reward steadfastness can, if aimed without care, dignify what should be condemned. Where a formation's record is in the least doubt, restraint is the responsible posture. The broad citation distributes recognition without elevating any single command as the war's example; the refusal admits that, with losses heavy and the record contested, honours can ring hollow — and that for Herceg-Bosna, whose legitimacy was itself disputed, a misplaced honour compounded the doubt.

The ambivalence is real and morally charged. The citation that raises one command's morale lowers another's and risks attaching the leadership's name to acts it should disavow; the broad gesture inspires little; the refusal reads as coldness to soldiers who expected acknowledgement. The safest honour was often the one withheld.

This is a recurring leadership choice rather than a single decorated event; the Codex holds the most recent decision and the engine binds the shared families — honour one, honour broadly, or decline — not any particular unit. It moves cohesion and morale, not the territory. The honest reading is that an HVO decoration was a gesture whose symbolic cost could outrun its morale benefit, and that to honour without scrutiny was to risk honouring what the record would not bear.
